paragraphs.text: A festival of martyrs has brought us together, but it was longing for Christ and his grace that gathered us. Out of love for our Lord Jesus Christ let us hurry to honor the martyrs, for whoever honors martyrs loves Christ. If "whoever receives you receives me," then whoever honors martyrs honors the one to whom they bore witness. The martyrs are remembered and Christ is glorified, for remembering the martyrs is an honor to Christ. And when martyrs are being commemorated, the commemoration cannot pass without praises.

For "the memory of the righteous is with praises." Martyrs are praised, not so that they may receive the praise, but so that through the praises we may take up their zeal. This is why the saints are praised: so that zeal for what is praised may lead those who contend for piety to self-control. For the praise of a righteous man is nothing other than the gladness of those who hear it, as Scripture says: "When the righteous are praised, the peoples rejoice."

The ungodly die and the godly die. Both share the name of death, but the difference is great and the gap between them is great. The death of the righteous is precious to the Master, as it says: "Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of his holy ones." Do you see the death of the righteous honored by God? See also the death of the ungodly condemned by all, as David testifies when he says: "The death of sinners is evil." The death of the righteous and of the martyrs is precious to God, not because their bodies are dissolved, but because their contests are brought to completion. The righteous and the unrighteous have tasted the same death. Both have been afflicted, but the one as a training in righteousness, the other as a rebuke of sin. This is why Scripture calls the sufferings of the righteous "afflictions" and those of sinners "scourges." Of the righteous it says: "Many are the afflictions of the righteous, and the Lord will deliver them out of them all"; and of the ungodly: "Many are the scourges of the sinner." The afflictions are many and the scourges are many. But the afflictions have as their physician the very one for whose sake they are endured, while the scourges of the ungodly have no consolation, unless repentance should somehow snatch them away from punishment.

The death of martyrs is the honor of immortal glory. The death of martyrs has exposed the tyranny of death to public shame. When our Savior had led his victory over death in triumph, the great bodyguards and soldiers followed in the footsteps of the great King, and like their Master they won the victory over death, trampling down death by death and quenching the flame of death with their blood.

I call the sides of the martyrs blessed. The martyrs are blessed in every part, but a limb that becomes an instrument of virtue has a greater blessedness. The righteous man is blessed as a whole, for "Blessed is the man who fears the Lord"; yet within that whole the members that serve the virtues receive a special distinction. So the Savior says to the apostles: "Blessed are your eyes, for they see, and your ears, for they hear." The eyes of the righteous had become instruments of virtue: they had attended well to the Savior's dispensation, had looked on the temple from outside, and with the eye of the soul had seen the God who dwelt within the temple. "Blessed then are your eyes, for they see" means "for they understand." If blessedness came simply from seeing the Savior, why are the Jews not blessed? They saw him with the eyes of sense. But because they saw the body and did not perceive the God in the body, they are shut out of the blessing.

So the apostles' eyes are blessed, "for they see." In Scripture, to "see" is to be illumined in the mind's eye of the soul and to behold the depths of the truth. That is why in ancient times they called the prophets "seers": not because other people were blind, but because the prophets truly beheld the depths of the truth. So when Saul, the king, was about to come to the kingship and had gone out to look for his father's donkeys, he asked one of the people going out of the city, "Is the seer here?", which means, "Is the prophet here?" And elsewhere a man who set himself up as a prophet against the prophet Amos said: "Seer, go, flee to the land of Judah, live there, and prophesy there."
Only those who know God see rightly. And God is seen not with the eyes of the flesh but with a pure heart, as it says: "Blessed are the pure in heart, for they shall see God."

So the Savior calls blessed the instruments of virtue in the body: eyes that see well and ears that hear with discernment. Blessed are the ears, not of those who merely hear well, but of those who receive with understanding. Having heard, one must understand, and having understood, one must obey, as it is written: "Hear, daughter, and see, and incline your ear," meaning "Obey and understand."

So every member of the martyrs is called blessed. Their eyes, both of body and of soul, beheld God rightly: the eyes of the body because they recognized the Creator from his creation, and the eyes of the mind because they beheld God in purity of heart. Their ears too became blessed, receiving the divine words. Just as a cistern slopes toward a flowing pipe, so the hearing of the righteous man inclines toward the streams of the divine law, as it says: "I will incline my ear to a parable." Why "incline"? Because every pitcher that receives water receives it when tilted, and so every hearing that inclines itself toward obedience receives the streams of the divine word.

I also call their sides blessed, which took on the unconquerable side of piety: they were scraped, yet they did not scour away their piety. It was not for nothing, brothers, that the tortures of the righteous were everywhere aimed at their sides, since sin came from a side. By sin I do not mean the woman who came from the side, but the sin that entered through her. The thing God created does not have the nature of sin; rather, the evil of sin came in through a turning away. Still, since the side became the cause of sin, the martyrs had the very members from which sin sprang scraped away. For this reason the Savior on the cross also received the lance in his side, and from it came blood and water, for the cleansing of souls and the sanctification of bodies. So in the case of men a particular member is often called blessed in this way, just as blessed Mary was also called blessed when someone said: "Blessed is the womb that bore you and the breasts that nursed you."

Blessed are the feet of the martyrs, which did not turn aside from the truth, which allowed the martyrs to say: "Establish my steps in your paths," and again: "My foot has stood on level ground." And just as the members of the righteous are praised one by one, so too the members of the ungodly are exposed and pitied one by one, as when David says: "Let not the foot of pride come against me, and let not the hand of the sinner shake me." He showed the whole by means of a part. What does "Let not the foot of pride come against me" mean? It means: "Let not the way of sin brush against me." And "Let not the hand of the sinner shake me"? He means the deeds of the sinner. Since the power of action lies in the hand and the power of movement in the foot, he is saying: "Let no deed of sin approach me, and let me not go on to advance in sin."

This is why blessed Moses was commanded by God to take the blood of the lamb of the peace offering and put it on the tip of the priest's right ear, on the tip of his right hand, and on the tip of his right foot. The divine word all but teaches us that these three members must be fitted for virtue: the ear, because hearing has become the vessel of the divine word; the hand, because action follows hearing; and the foot, because after action comes progress in action. Today too, take the precious blood from the sacrifice of the martyrs and anoint your hearing with it, so that you may learn to listen well to the Gospels. The hearing of heretics needs this anointing, so that they may understand the sayings of the Gospel and not slander what is holy. For unless the ears of those who know wrongly receive this seal, they cannot understand.

But let us come to the very fountain of cleansing, the fountain of wisdom that cleanses us and waters us. The divine fountain of the Gospel does two things: it gives drink and it cleanses. It gives drink to thirsty souls, and it cleanses filthy minds. Are you filthy with sin? Come to the fountain and be cleansed. Do you thirst for the word of piety? Come to Christ and drink. For his is the voice that says: "If anyone thirsts, let him come to me and drink." And his again is the promise: "You are already clean because of the word I have spoken to you."

And again the same Savior, promising a great reward to those who succeed in piety, says: "Blessed are those who are persecuted for righteousness' sake," and: "Blessed are you when they revile you and persecute you and falsely say every evil word against you on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." Much and little are not measured by the word itself but by the standing of the one who speaks it. What I mean is this: what is much to me is not much to a rich man; what is much to a private citizen is little to a ruler. The wealth of rulers is nothing compared with the royal treasuries. Or, to go step by step: a peasant's wealth is nothing beside a townsman's household, a townsman's wealth is nothing beside a ruler's, and a ruler's wealth is nothing beside the royal treasuries. Let us see, then, who promised the great reward. If it were a prophet, he might, being a man, have thought something much; if an apostle, he might, being a man, have thought a little thing much. But who is it that says it is much? The one who holds the eternal treasures, the one who has the wealth that surpasses all understanding.

I find two things in Scripture that can train us in piety: the same reward is promised to those who are reviled for piety and to those who despise glory. It is possible to receive the reward without persecution. For instance, someone who has despised honor and glory can be equal to someone who has despised persecutions and afflictions. Hear how this is, with the words "the reward is great." I see it said once in the Old Testament and once in the New; and though I have searched, I find a "great reward" mentioned nowhere else than once in the Gospel and once in the Old Testament.

The New Testament, then, speaks of a reward stored up for the persecuted. "Blessed are you," it says, "when they revile you and persecute you and falsely say every evil word against you on my account. Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." Great is the reward for the martyrs who are afflicted, for those who shed their blood, for those who live ascetic lives for piety's sake, for those who endure fasting, for those who bear affliction and every hardship for piety's sake.

The great reward he promised to those afflicted for piety he also promises to Abraham as he trampled on human glory. With his own household servants Abraham routed the kings of the Assyrians. By faith he overcame the kings and took from them the captives of Sodom, Gomorrah, and the Pentapolis (for these cities were still standing then). The five kings had been defeated, but the great victor, made great by faith, proved stronger than those who had conquered them. He took from the enemy all the captives, the women and children carried off from Sodom, and returned with everything. Then the defeated kings of Sodom and Gomorrah came out to meet the victor, and since he had given them deliverance and rescued their wives and children from captivity, they said to him as to a conqueror: "Have the horse as a reward for your labors on our behalf," meaning all the cavalry. "Take all our horses," they say, "and the gold and the silver; only give us the women and children." Then blessed Abraham, refusing glory from men and unwilling to receive wages from men for his own labors, says: "I will stretch out my hands to God Most High, who made heaven and earth, that I will not take anything, from a thread to a sandal strap," so that no one may say, "I made Abraham rich." As if to say: "I have the one who makes me rich, and I have no need of a beggar's wealth." What then? As soon as he had rejected the honor that comes from men, Scripture says, hardly a syllable later: "And God said to Abraham: Do not fear, Abraham; your reward shall be very great."

"Rejoice and be glad, for your reward is great in heaven." In these exact words, I say, it occurs once in the Old Testament and once in the New. But David says the same thing elsewhere with the same meaning: "In keeping them there is great recompense," that is, "the reward is great."

See how great a reward the martyrs are counted worthy of, and how great a reward you too are counted worthy of when you put the things of God before human things. "I will not take anything, from a thread to a sandal strap." What is the word used here for "strap"? It is what we call, to use the everyday word, a thong. Why is it called by a word meaning "rounded"? Because the craftsman often works the leather into a circle and then cuts it. We are explaining a word from an ordinary trade; but Paul actually did the work, though in those days he worked on dead hides. Afterward, by the power of the Spirit, he cut down the thoughts of demons. Throwing away the knife of his trade, he took up the sword of the Spirit and cut through all the thoughts of the ungodly, as you can hear him say: "For the weapons of our warfare are not fleshly, but powerful for God, tearing down arguments and every proud height raised up against the knowledge of God."

Having taken up this sword, the apostles are to judge on the twelve thrones. For when they judge, they must also have a sword: the judge does not bear the sword in vain. The sword of judges is forged iron; the sword of the apostles is the word of wisdom. God will judge the world through the saints; at that time he will entrust the judgment of the world to the righteous. The twelve will judge the twelve tribes of Israel. Paul too, the herald of the world, will judge the world; and not Paul alone, but also those who share his mind. Hear him say: "Do you not know that the saints will judge the world? And if the world is to be judged by you, are you unworthy to judge the smallest matters?" The righteous are the judges of the world; the saints are the judges of the world.

The Old Testament did not leave this out either. As if recording beforehand the future coming of the Savior, it introduces the righteous, saying: "The high praises of God are in their throats, and two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance on the nations and rebukes on the peoples, to bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles, to carry out on them the judgment that is written." What judgment? The one written in the words: "You will sit on twelve thrones, judging the twelve tribes of Israel"—"to carry out on them the judgment that is written." And notice the distinction. At that time the righteous will judge the world: the holy prophets and apostles who cultivated the world with the divine word. And what does it say? "Two-edged swords," meaning divine words. For the righteous will judge by the word: "For the word is living and active and sharper than any two-edged sword."

"And two-edged swords in their hands, to execute vengeance on the nations and rebukes on the peoples." Vengeance on the nations is one thing, and rebuke of the peoples is another. Pay attention, I beg you. He calls "nations" those who have remained in paganism and have not received the glory of Christ. On them is vengeance, as the Savior says: "But as for these enemies of mine, who did not want me to reign over them, bring them here and slaughter them before me."

"To execute vengeance on the nations"—those who have utterly refused to believe—"and rebukes on the peoples." By "peoples" he means those who were unwilling to come to full knowledge. On these he does not take vengeance as on enemies; rather, as their Master, he rebukes them, examining their sins.

"To bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles"—the kings of those unbelieving nations, not of those who have walked in piety. For those who reign with piety reign both in the present age and in the age to come. "If you delight," it says, "O kings and rulers, in reigning forever, honor wisdom, so that you may reign forever."

"To bind their kings in fetters." Picture, brother, the persecutors fettered by their sin. Picture those who receive authority to judge the ones who judged them and to torment the ones who tormented them. Picture the tyrant who once sat on the tribunal now standing before the martyr, and the martyr showing his own side and saying: "Was it not this side that you tore apart? Was it not this neck of mine that you cut off? What charge did you have against me? For what sacrilege, for what wrong did you pass such a sentence? You received from God the authority to judge, and you poured out your wrath on the servants of God."

"In fetters and iron manacles," it says, so that both feet and hands are bound, since it says "in fetters and manacles." Fetters secure the feet; manacles secure the hands. For the Savior pronounced just such a sentence: "Bind his hands and feet," he says, "and throw him into the outer darkness." In keeping with this the prophet also says: "To bind their kings in fetters and their nobles in iron manacles, and to carry out on them the judgment that is written."

And when these things have happened, what will follow? "This is the glory of all his holy ones," it says. It is glory enough for the saints, he means, to judge those who judged them, to bind those who bound them, to hand over to the eternal tribunal those who subjected holy souls to an unjust tribunal. Such are the things the martyrs will say as they display their marks, which they endured for Christ. That is why Paul says: "From now on let no one trouble me, for I bear on my body the marks of Christ." Just as the saints can glory in those victorious wounds, so too the ungodly will then see the great reversal: the captives in glory, the judged now judging, the tortured handing over the wicked rulers and the ungodly powerful to eternal punishment. They will be struck to the soul as they call to mind what they dared to do, and they will say—not the tales people invent today, but what the divine Scripture says: "Then the righteous man will stand with great boldness before the face of those who afflicted him, and when they see him they will say to one another: Is this not the one we once held in derision, fools that we were? We thought his life madness and his end without honor. How has he now been counted among the sons of God, and how is his lot among the saints?"

When that glory appears, consider how great the joy of the righteous will be, and how great the torment of the unrighteous. Do not imagine that their torment will then touch them as much as their shame. The shame alone is enough, in place of any punishment. And for the righteous, the very joy of the kingdom is enough, in place of the kingdom itself.

Then Paul will stand by, then Isaiah will come. Think, brothers, of how we make promises to people who have never yet seen a great city: "Come, and you will see a great city, with public baths surpassing all others in beauty and size." Then, when the other is at last granted to come to the place, the one who promised the sight beforehand begins to take pride in it and say: "Did I lie? Didn't I show you?" And just as someone who knows the city plays host to the stranger, shows him what he did not know, and says, "This is the place I told you about; this is the place I taught you about," so too at that time the righteous will stand beside those who have been brought into the kingdom.

Then Isaiah will begin to say: "Did I lie when I said that then they would rejoice and have praise upon their heads? Here sighing has fled away, and grief has fled away." And again the same Isaiah will say to the others: "Come, and I will show you the one you worshiped, whom you loved without knowing him and revered by faith. Come, I will show you, using the words of the prophets: 'Behold our God, in whom we rejoiced and hoped.'" Then those who see will say: "Lord, from of old we have not heard, nor have our eyes seen any God but you."

David too will begin to say: "I too, as a king, will show you where he sits who is descended from me and is my Master. See where he sits, of whom I truthfully said: 'The Lord said to my Lord: Sit at my right hand.'" Paul too will stand by and say: "Allow me as well; I will show you that my words were true. See the Savior far above every rule and authority and dominion and every name that is named." Then those being shown around will ask: "Who is this choir of shining ones?" "These," he says, "are the prophets. These who glitter are the apostles. These flashing with their wounds are the martyrs. These who flourish are the ascetics. These harvesting paradise are those who fasted. And to put it briefly, all these, this whole crowd, the living choir that has entered into eternal life, is the one who toiled for piety, as David says: 'And he toiled forever, and he shall live to the end.'" This is how the servants of God are shown around when they enter that kingdom.

Again, those who have gone before wait for those who depart from here, when the soul of a righteous person leaves this world, escorted by the hands of holy angels. The angels bring it into the royal city, for the Jerusalem above is the only city that truly reigns, and they stand there as if in a harbour. Seeing them, those who went before say: “These ships, where have they come from? What have they brought? What trade have they done?” The righteous who went before say this as they watch, as if in a harbour within the kingdom, those who come in from this life so full of groaning and so tossed by waves, bringing their ships in unharmed. For instance, to set it out as a picture: at that time those who came before Job asked, “What cargo has this ship brought?” “It is full of patience,” comes the answer. David’s ship came in, and those at the harbour ask, “What does this ship carry?” They hear from the divine power that it carries a cargo of meekness. Joseph, what did he come bearing? A cargo of chastity. What did Daniel come bearing? A cargo of wisdom. So they traded in different gifts. One traded in faith; or rather, none of them traded in anything without faith. Another traded in chastity; one in patience, another in the sufferings of martyrdom; another brought the profit of the ascetic life, another of fasting, another of keeping vigil, another of almsgiving and love for the poor. For you know that a merchant who cannot find a way to buy cheap and sell dear does not go into trade. Even if he often sees that a line of business is enough to feed him but brings in no profit, he says, “This does not feed me.” So you too, when you trade in righteousness, if you know you are too weak to sell, say, “This does not save me. Whatever brings me the better profit, that is what I will trade in.” I will show you how virtue is bought cheap here and sold dear. What is easier to come by than cold water? See how cheap the virtues are! With a cup of cold water and a piece of bread you can buy the kingdom of heaven. May we all attain it, by the grace and love for humankind of our Lord Jesus Christ, to whom be glory and power for ever and ever. Amen.
